questions.stem:
An ACL applied inbound on a router interface contains:

access-list 120 permit tcp any any eq 443
access-list 120 deny tcp host 10.1.1.50 any eq 443

Host 10.1.1.50 sends HTTPS traffic in through that interface. What happens, and why?

options.text: It is permitted, because the first entry matches and processing stops at the first match
options.rationale: Correct: the broad permit matches before the deny is ever checked.

options.text: It is denied, because the more specific entry always wins
options.rationale: ACLs don't rank entries by specificity; order decides.

options.text: It is denied by the implicit deny at the end
options.rationale: The implicit deny applies only when no entry matches, and the first entry matches.

options.text: It is permitted only after both entries have been checked
options.rationale: Processing stops at the first match.

questions.explanation: ACLs are processed top-down, the first match wins, and an implicit deny follows the last entry. A broad entry placed above a specific one hides it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Top-down, first match wins; implicit deny at the end.

questions.stem: Traffic from the 10.20.0.0/16 sales network must be kept away from the HR server subnet, but sales must still reach everything else. If a standard ACL is used, where should it be placed, and why?

options.text: Close to the destination, on the interface toward the HR subnet, because a standard ACL matches only the source and would block sales from everything if placed near it
options.rationale: Correct: near the destination it affects only traffic heading to HR.

options.text: Close to the source, on the sales network's interface, to stop the traffic early
options.rationale: With only a source to match, it would block sales traffic to every destination.

options.text: On every router interface
options.rationale: That blocks sales everywhere and adds needless processing.

options.text: Anywhere, because placement doesn't matter for standard ACLs
options.rationale: Placement matters a great deal, because a standard ACL can't see the destination.

questions.explanation: Standard ACLs filter on source IP only (numbers 1-99 and 1300-1999). Because they can't see the destination, they are placed close to the destination.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACLs see only the source, so they go close to the destination.

questions.stem: Which wildcard mask matches every address in 172.16.8.0/22?

options.rationale: Correct: a /22 subnet mask is 255.255.252.0, and its inverse is 0.0.3.255.
That is the subnet mask, not the wildcard mask.
That matches a /24 only.
That matches a /16, far wider than the /22.

questions.explanation: Wildcard masking is an inverse mask: a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored. Invert the subnet mask (255.255.252.0) to get 0.0.3.255.
questions.discriminator_tested: A wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask.

questions.stem: Policy says: block only Telnet (TCP 23) from the 10.1.1.0/24 lab to the server 10.9.9.10, and allow all other traffic. Which ACL type can express this, and where should it be placed?

options.text: An extended ACL, placed close to the source
options.rationale: Correct: it can match source, destination, protocol, and port, so it can stop the traffic early without side effects.

options.text: A standard ACL, placed close to the destination
options.rationale: A standard ACL can't match the destination or the Telnet port.

options.text: A standard ACL, placed close to the source
options.rationale: It would block all lab traffic, not just Telnet to one server.

options.text: An extended ACL, which must always be placed at the destination
options.rationale: Extended ACLs are precise enough to go close to the source.

questions.explanation: Extended ACLs filter on source, destination, protocol, and ports (numbers 100-199 and 2000-2699). Because they are so granular, they are placed close to the source.
questions.discriminator_tested: Extended ACLs are granular, so they go close to the source.

questions.stem: A router ACL permits outbound web requests, but the replies are dropped unless a matching inbound entry is added. What do stateful firewalls add that this ACL lacks?

options.text: Session awareness: they track connections and allow the return traffic automatically
options.rationale: Correct: an ACL judges each packet with no memory of sessions.

options.text: Encryption of the traffic
options.rationale: Encryption is a VPN function, not what separates firewalls from ACLs.

options.text: Faster first-match processing
options.rationale: Speed is not the difference; session tracking is.

options.text: Support for wildcard masks
options.rationale: ACLs already use wildcard masks.

questions.explanation: Firewalls enforce policy between networks and add session awareness beyond ACL filtering. ACLs are stateless filters; stateful firewalls track sessions.
questions.discriminator_tested: ACLs are stateless; stateful firewalls track sessions.

questions.stem: A laptop's disk is fully encrypted. Which threat does this encryption, by itself, address?

options.text: Someone reading the data after stealing the laptop
options.rationale: Correct: encryption provides confidentiality.

options.text: Someone altering files without anyone noticing
options.rationale: Detecting changes is integrity, which needs hashing or signatures.

options.text: Proving who wrote a particular file
options.rationale: Proving identity is authentication.

options.text: The laptop becoming unavailable when its disk fails
options.rationale: Availability needs backups or redundancy.

questions.explanation: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext with an algorithm and a key. It provides confidentiality, but not integrity or authentication on its own.
questions.discriminator_tested: Encryption provides confidentiality, not integrity or authentication on its own.

questions.stem: Two branch routers encrypt bulk traffic with AES, using the same secret key at both ends. What is the main challenge of this kind of symmetric key encryption?

options.text: Getting the shared key to both ends securely
options.rationale: Correct: key distribution is the classic problem with symmetric encryption.

options.text: It is too slow for bulk data
options.rationale: Symmetric ciphers are fast, which is why they are used for bulk data.

options.text: Each end needs a different key
options.rationale: Using the same key at both ends is what makes it symmetric.

options.text: It can encrypt but never decrypt
options.rationale: The same key both encrypts and decrypts.

questions.explanation: Symmetric key encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suits bulk data, but distributing the key securely is the challenge.
questions.discriminator_tested: Symmetric: same key, fast; key distribution is the challenge.

questions.stem: Why must DES never be used in new deployments?

options.text: Its 56-bit key is short enough to brute-force, so it is obsolete and insecure
options.rationale: Correct: modern hardware can try every possible key.

options.text: It is a hash function, not a cipher
options.rationale: DES is a symmetric block cipher.

options.text: It uses public and private key pairs
options.rationale: DES is symmetric.

options.text: It can encrypt only text files
options.rationale: DES encrypts any data in 64-bit blocks.

questions.explanation: DES uses a 56-bit key and 64-bit blocks. The key is far too short for today's computing power, so DES is obsolete and insecure.
questions.discriminator_tested: DES: 56-bit key, obsolete and insecure.

questions.stem: Why was 3DES introduced, and why is it now deprecated?

options.text: It applied DES three times as a stopgap for DES's short key; it is slow and has been replaced by AES
options.rationale: Correct: it was a stopgap that has since been superseded.

options.text: It is a hash that replaced MD5; it is deprecated because its digests are too long
options.rationale: 3DES is a cipher, not a hash.

options.text: It replaced AES because AES was broken
options.rationale: AES is the current standard; 3DES came before it.

options.text: It is DES with larger 168-bit blocks
options.rationale: 3DES keeps DES's 64-bit blocks and runs DES three times.

questions.explanation: 3DES applies DES three times. It was a stopgap, is slow, and has been replaced by AES.
questions.discriminator_tested: 3DES: deprecated, slow stopgap, replaced by AES.

questions.stem: A team must choose a symmetric cipher to encrypt its backup archives. The options are DES, 3DES, AES-256, and MD5. Which should it choose?

options.text: AES-256
options.rationale: Correct: AES is the current standard symmetric cipher.

options.text: DES
options.rationale: DES is obsolete and insecure.

options.text: 3DES
options.rationale: 3DES is a deprecated, slow stopgap.

options.text: MD5
options.rationale: MD5 is a (broken) hash function, not a cipher.

questions.explanation: AES, with 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys, is the current standard symmetric cipher. DES and 3DES are obsolete or deprecated, and MD5 doesn't encrypt at all.
questions.discriminator_tested: AES is the current standard symmetric cipher.

questions.stem: A download page lists a file's SHA-256 value. A user computes the SHA-256 hash of the downloaded file, and it matches. What does the match show, and why isn't hashing a form of encryption?

options.text: The file was not altered; hashes are one-way and can't be reversed to recover the data
options.rationale: Correct: hashing verifies integrity and has no decryption.

options.text: The file is now encrypted on the user's disk
options.rationale: Computing a hash changes nothing about the file.

options.text: It proves who published the file
options.rationale: Proving the publisher needs a digital signature; anyone can post a hash value.

options.text: The hash can be decrypted with the publisher's key to rebuild the file
options.rationale: Hashes are one-way; nothing can turn one back into the data.

questions.explanation: Hashes are one-way functions that produce a fixed-length digest. They verify integrity, and because they can't be reversed, hashing is not encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hashes verify integrity; they are one-way, so they are not encryption.

questions.stem: A developer proposes MD5 for verifying the integrity of security-critical firmware updates. What is the problem with this choice?

options.text: MD5 is broken: an attacker can craft a different file with the same digest, so SHA-256 or longer should be used
options.rationale: Correct: MD5 collisions make it unfit for security use.

options.text: MD5 is too slow for large files
options.rationale: MD5 is fast; the problem is that it is broken.

options.text: MD5 is an encryption algorithm, not a hash
options.rationale: MD5 is a hash function.

options.text: MD5 produces a 512-bit digest that is too large to store
options.rationale: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest.

questions.explanation: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest, but practical collisions have been shown. That makes it broken for security use; SHA-256 or longer is preferred.
questions.discriminator_tested: MD5 is broken (collisions); avoid it for security use.

questions.stem: Which statement about the SHA family of hash algorithms is NOT true?

options.text: SHA-1 is the recommended choice for new systems
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: SHA-1 is deprecated.

options.text: SHA-256 or longer is preferred
options.rationale: True.

options.text: SHA-2 and SHA-3 are members of the family
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Each algorithm produces a fixed-length digest
options.rationale: True: that is how hash functions work.

questions.explanation: The Secure Hash Algorithm family includes SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. SHA-1 is deprecated; SHA-256 or longer is preferred.
questions.discriminator_tested: SHA-1 is deprecated; use SHA-256 or longer.

questions.stem: A traveling salesperson connects to headquarters from hotel rooms. Separately, two branch offices are permanently linked over the internet. Which VPN use cases are these?

options.text: Remote access (user to site) for the salesperson; site-to-site for the branches
options.rationale: Correct: one user versus two whole networks.

options.text: Site-to-site for the salesperson; remote access for the branches
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both are site-to-site
options.rationale: The salesperson is a single user, not a site.

options.text: Both are provider-managed MPLS VPNs
options.rationale: Nothing says a provider runs either one.

questions.explanation: A VPN is an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet. Its main use cases are remote access (user to site) and site-to-site, and it is cheaper than leased lines.
questions.discriminator_tested: Remote access = user to site; site-to-site = network to network.

questions.stem: What most clearly separates enterprise VPNs from provider-managed VPNs?

options.text: The organization itself builds and manages an enterprise VPN, such as IPsec or SSL VPN, and controls its security
options.rationale: Correct: the customer controls the security.

options.text: Enterprise VPNs always run over MPLS
options.rationale: MPLS is typical of provider-managed VPNs.

options.text: Provider-managed VPNs are always encrypted, while enterprise VPNs are not
options.rationale: A provider isolates traffic but doesn't necessarily encrypt it.

options.text: Enterprise VPNs can't cross the internet
options.rationale: Enterprise VPNs normally run over the internet.

questions.explanation: Enterprise VPNs are built and managed by the organization, typically IPsec or SSL VPN over the internet, so the customer controls the security. With provider-managed VPNs, the service provider runs it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enterprise VPN = customer-controlled security.

questions.stem: A company moves its branch links to an MPLS-based VPN service run by its carrier. A manager assumes all branch traffic is now encrypted. Is that right?

options.text: Not necessarily: the provider keeps each customer's traffic separate but doesn't necessarily encrypt it
options.rationale: Correct: isolation is not encryption.

options.text: Yes: MPLS always encrypts traffic with AES
options.rationale: MPLS labels and separates traffic; it does not encrypt it.

options.text: Yes: the provider automatically runs IPsec for every customer
options.rationale: Encryption is not automatic; the customer may need to add it.

options.text: No: MPLS VPNs send traffic over the public internet with no separation
options.rationale: The provider does separate customer traffic.

questions.explanation: With provider-managed VPNs, such as MPLS-based ones, the service provider isolates customer traffic, but that traffic is not necessarily encrypted. Customers who need confidentiality add their own encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: Provider-managed VPNs isolate traffic but don't necessarily encrypt it.

questions.stem: Which statement about IPsec is NOT true?

options.text: It is a single protocol with one fixed algorithm
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: IPsec is a framework of protocols and algorithms.

options.text: It can provide confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay protection
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It uses IKE to negotiate its security parameters
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It uses AH and/or ESP to protect packets
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: IPsec is a suite that secures IP traffic with confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay. It is a framework (IKE plus AH/ESP), not a single protocol.
questions.discriminator_tested: IPsec is a framework, not a single protocol.

questions.stem: When Cisco IOS IPsec brings up a tunnel, what do IKE phase 1 and IKE phase 2 each establish, in order?

options.text: Phase 1 builds a secure management channel between the peers; phase 2 then builds the security associations that protect the data
options.rationale: Correct: first the management channel, then the data SAs.

options.text: Phase 1 protects the user data; phase 2 builds the management channel
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Phase 1 applies the crypto map; phase 2 creates the transform set
options.rationale: These are configuration items, not IKE negotiation phases.

options.text: Both phases encrypt user data, with no separate management channel
options.rationale: Phase 1 exists to create the protected management channel.

questions.explanation: Cisco IOS IPsec is configured with an IKE policy, a transform set, and a crypto map or profile on an interface. IKE phase 1 builds the secure management channel, then phase 2 builds the data SAs.
questions.discriminator_tested: IKE phase 1 = management channel; phase 2 = data SAs.

questions.stem: Two sites must keep their traffic confidential as it crosses the internet. Which IPsec security protocol is required?

options.text: ESP (IP protocol 50)
options.rationale: Correct: ESP provides encryption plus integrity and authentication.

options.text: AH (IP protocol 51)
options.rationale: AH provides integrity and authentication but no encryption.

options.text: GRE (IP protocol 47)
options.rationale: GRE is not part of IPsec and doesn't encrypt.

options.text: AH with a longer key
options.rationale: AH never encrypts, whatever the key length.

questions.explanation: Of the IPsec security protocols, AH (protocol 51) provides integrity and authentication only. ESP (protocol 50) adds encryption, so it is the one that provides confidentiality.
questions.discriminator_tested: AH does not encrypt; ESP does.

questions.stem: Two branch routers protect the traffic between their LANs. The original packets, including the PCs' private IP headers, must be hidden in transit. Which IPsec encryption mode fits?

options.text: ESP in tunnel mode
options.rationale: Correct: the whole original packet is encapsulated and encrypted.

options.text: ESP in transport mode
options.rationale: Transport mode protects only the payload and leaves the original IP header visible.

options.text: AH in transport mode
options.rationale: AH doesn't encrypt at all.

options.text: GRE alone
options.rationale: GRE encapsulates without encrypting.

questions.explanation: IPsec encryption uses ESP with symmetric ciphers (AES preferred), with keys negotiated through IKE and Diffie-Hellman. Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet and is typical for site-to-site; transport mode protects only the payload.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tunnel = whole packet (site-to-site); transport = payload only.

questions.stem: Two sites need to run OSPF, a routing protocol that uses multicast, across a tunnel over a private provider link. Encryption is not required. Which tunnel type fits?

options.text: A GRE tunnel
options.rationale: Correct: GRE carries multicast and routing protocols.

options.text: A crypto-map IPsec tunnel on its own
options.rationale: Crypto-map IPsec carries unicast IP only, not multicast routing traffic.

options.text: AH in transport mode
options.rationale: AH adds integrity, not a multicast-capable tunnel.

options.text: An SSL VPN for remote users
options.rationale: That connects individual users, not two routers running OSPF.

questions.explanation: GRE tunnels use IP protocol 47 and can carry many protocols, including multicast and routing protocols. They are flexible but provide no encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE is flexible (multicast, routing) but has no encryption.

questions.stem: Two sites must run OSPF over the internet, and all traffic must be encrypted. Why is GRE over IPsec a common answer?

options.text: GRE carries the multicast routing traffic; IPsec adds the encryption
options.rationale: Correct: each protocol covers what the other lacks.

options.text: GRE adds the encryption; IPsec adds multicast support
options.rationale: This reverses their roles.

options.text: GRE alone encrypts, so IPsec is optional
options.rationale: GRE provides no encryption.

options.text: IPsec with crypto maps handles both, so GRE adds nothing
options.rationale: Crypto-map IPsec doesn't carry multicast routing protocols.

questions.explanation: In GRE over IPsec, a GRE tunnel is protected by IPsec. GRE adds multiprotocol and multicast support; IPsec adds encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE adds multicast and multiprotocol support; IPsec adds encryption.

questions.stem: A company with 120 branches wants a hub-and-spoke VPN in which branches can also build tunnels to each other on demand, without configuring a full mesh by hand. Which Cisco solution fits?

options.text: DMVPN
options.rationale: Correct: hub-and-spoke with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels.

options.text: A static full mesh of point-to-point GRE tunnels
options.rationale: That is the hand-built full mesh the company wants to avoid; it doesn't scale.

options.text: A single IPsec VTI to headquarters
options.rationale: One VTI gives one point-to-point tunnel, with no dynamic spoke-to-spoke links.

options.text: An SSL VPN for each employee
options.rationale: That provides user remote access, not branch-to-branch networking.

questions.explanation: Cisco DMVPN is a hub-and-spoke VPN with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels, built from mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec. It scales without configuring a full mesh.
questions.discriminator_tested: DMVPN scales without configuring a full mesh.

questions.stem: What separates a Cisco IPsec VTI from a crypto-map-based IPsec configuration?

options.text: A VTI is a routable virtual interface (route-based, with no GRE header); crypto maps are policy-based and pick traffic with an ACL
options.rationale: Correct: route-based versus policy-based.

options.text: A VTI always adds a GRE header
options.rationale: A VTI needs no GRE header.

options.text: A VTI doesn't encrypt traffic
options.rationale: A VTI is an IPsec tunnel and encrypts.

options.text: Crypto maps are route-based; VTIs are policy-based
options.rationale: This is reversed.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI makes the IPsec tunnel a routable virtual interface. It is route-based with no GRE header, in contrast to policy-based crypto maps.
questions.discriminator_tested: VTI is route-based with no GRE header; crypto maps are policy-based.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a public key infrastructure (PKI)?

options.text: The whole framework of CAs, certificates, policies, and processes that bind public keys to identities
options.rationale: Correct: PKI is the complete trust system.

options.text: A single digital certificate
options.rationale: A certificate is one component of a PKI.

options.text: A symmetric cipher used for bulk encryption
options.rationale: PKI deals with public keys and identities, not bulk symmetric encryption.

options.text: One certificate authority server
options.rationale: A CA is one component; PKI includes the policies and processes around it.

questions.explanation: A public key infrastructure is the framework of CAs, certificates, policies, and processes that bind public keys to identities. It is the whole trust system, not any one component.
questions.discriminator_tested: PKI is the whole trust system, not one component.

questions.stem: A browser trusts a website's certificate because it was signed by an organization already in the browser's trusted list. What role does that organization play?

options.text: A certificate authority: the trust anchor that issued and signed the certificate
options.rationale: Correct: the CA signs certificates with its own private key.

options.text: A certificate template
options.rationale: A template is a set of issuing settings, not an organization.

options.text: A VPN concentrator
options.rationale: That terminates VPN tunnels; it doesn't vouch for websites.

options.text: A hash algorithm
options.rationale: A hash is a function, not a trusted organization.

questions.explanation: Certificate authorities are trusted entities that issue, sign, and revoke certificates. A CA is the trust anchor and signs with its own private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: The CA is the trust anchor and signs with its own private key.

questions.stem: An administrator wants every new web-server certificate issued with the same key usage, validity period, and key size, without setting them by hand each time. What does the CA use to apply these settings automatically?

options.text: A certificate template
options.rationale: Correct: a template is the blueprint the CA applies when issuing.

options.text: An existing certificate
options.rationale: A certificate is something that was issued, not the blueprint for future ones.

options.text: A certificate revocation list
options.rationale: A revocation list records cancelled certificates; it doesn't set issuing options.

options.text: The root CA's private key
options.rationale: The key signs certificates; it doesn't define their settings.

questions.explanation: A certificate template holds predefined settings (key usage, validity, key size, subject fields) that a CA applies when issuing certificates. It is the blueprint, not a certificate itself.
questions.discriminator_tested: A template is the blueprint for issuing, not a certificate.

questions.stem: Which statement about digital certificates is NOT true?

options.text: A certificate contains its owner's private key
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: certificates hold only the public key; the private key is never shared.

options.text: A certificate binds a public key to an identity
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Certificates commonly use the X.509 format
options.rationale: True.

options.text: A certificate is checked using the CA's signature, its validity dates, and its revocation status
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: Certificates are signed digital documents (X.509) that bind a public key to an identity. They hold the public key, never the private key, and are validated by the CA signature, dates, and revocation status.
questions.discriminator_tested: Certificates hold the public key, never the private key.

questions.stem:
To permit the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet, an administrator enters:

access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0

What is wrong with this standard ACL command?

options.text: A subnet mask was used where a wildcard mask is required; it should be 0.0.0.255
options.rationale: Correct: ACLs use inverse (wildcard) masks.

options.text: Standard ACLs need a protocol keyword such as 'ip'
options.rationale: Standard ACL entries have no protocol field.

options.text: 10 is an extended ACL number
options.rationale: 1-99 is the standard range.

options.text: A destination address is missing
options.rationale: Standard ACLs match the source only.

questions.explanation: Standard ACL commands take a number, an action, and a source with a wildcard, for example 'access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255'. There is no protocol or port.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACL commands: number, action, source plus wildcard.

questions.stem: Which command permits HTTP traffic from the 192.168.1.0/24 users to the web server 10.1.1.10?

options.text: access-list 110 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 80
options.rationale: Correct: action, protocol, source, destination, then port.

options.text: access-list 110 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 80 tcp
options.rationale: The protocol must come right after the action.

options.text: access-list 10 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 80
options.rationale: 10 is a standard ACL number, and standard ACLs can't match protocols or ports.

options.text: access-list 110 permit ip 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 80
options.rationale: 'ip' matches all traffic and can't take a port.

questions.explanation: Extended ACL commands follow the order: number, action, protocol, source (with wildcard), destination, then port. Port matching requires 'tcp' or 'udp'.
questions.discriminator_tested: Extended order: action, protocol, source, destination, then port.

questions.stem:
An administrator types:

ip access-list WEB-IN
 permit tcp any any eq 443

and the router rejects the first line. What is missing?

options.text: The 'standard' or 'extended' keyword; here it should be 'ip access-list extended WEB-IN'
options.rationale: Correct: named ACLs must state their type.

options.text: Named ACLs can't match TCP
options.rationale: An extended named ACL can match TCP and ports.

options.text: Each entry must begin with 'access-list'
options.rationale: Entries in a named ACL leave out the 'access-list' keyword.

options.text: ACL names must be numbers
options.rationale: Named ACLs exist precisely so a name can be used.

questions.explanation: Named ACLs are created with 'ip access-list standard NAME' or 'ip access-list extended NAME'. The keyword is required, and entries in ACL config mode omit 'access-list'.
questions.discriminator_tested: Named ACLs require the standard or extended keyword.

questions.stem: An administrator writes a careful extended ACL 150, but the traffic it should block still passes. 'show running-config' shows no 'ip access-group' command under any interface. Why is nothing being filtered?

options.text: The ACL was never applied to an interface, and an unapplied ACL filters nothing
options.rationale: Correct: it has to be applied with 'ip access-group' in a direction.

options.text: The implicit deny is turned off
options.rationale: The implicit deny can't be turned off, and it doesn't matter while the ACL is unapplied.

options.text: Extended ACLs must be applied with 'access-class'
options.rationale: 'access-class' is for VTY lines; interfaces use 'ip access-group'.

options.text: The router must be rebooted before ACLs take effect
options.rationale: Applied ACLs take effect immediately.

questions.explanation: Applying an ACL to an interface uses 'ip access-group 150 in' (or 'out') under the interface. An unapplied ACL filters nothing, and direction is relative to the router.
questions.discriminator_tested: An unapplied ACL filters nothing.

questions.stem:
To allow SSH management of a router only from 10.0.0.0/24, an administrator creates:

access-list 5 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255

Which commands apply it correctly?

options.text: line vty 0 4, then access-class 5 in
options.rationale: Correct: 'access-class' on the VTY lines limits management sessions to the device.

options.text: interface g0/0, then ip access-group 5 in
options.rationale: That filters all traffic passing through the interface, not specifically management sessions to the router.

options.text: line vty 0 4, then ip access-group 5 in
options.rationale: 'ip access-group' is an interface command, not a line command.

options.text: interface g0/0, then access-class 5 in
options.rationale: 'access-class' belongs under the VTY lines.

questions.explanation: Applying an ACL to VTY lines uses 'line vty 0 4' and 'access-class 5 in'. 'access-class' limits management sessions to the device; 'ip access-group' filters traffic through an interface.
questions.discriminator_tested: 'access-class' = VTY management access; 'ip access-group' = interface traffic.

questions.stem:
A named ACL is applied, but Telnet to 10.5.5.5 is still allowed:

ip access-list extended BRANCH
 10 permit ip any any
 20 deny tcp any host 10.5.5.5 eq 23

Why?

options.text: The broad permit at sequence 10 matches first and shadows the deny; the deny needs a lower sequence number, such as 5
options.rationale: Correct: order decides, and the first match wins.

options.text: The implicit deny overrides sequence 20
options.rationale: The implicit deny is only reached when nothing matches; sequence 10 already matched.

options.text: A deny entry only works with the 'log' keyword
options.rationale: 'log' only records matches; it doesn't change them.

options.text: Telnet uses TCP 22, so the port is wrong
options.rationale: Telnet uses TCP 23; SSH uses 22.

questions.explanation: Entry order and sequence numbers decide behavior. A broad entry above a specific one shadows it, and sequence numbers in a named ACL let you insert the deny above the permit.
questions.discriminator_tested: A broad entry above a specific one shadows it.

questions.stem:
The router rejects this command:

access-list 120 deny ip any any eq 23

Why?

options.text: Ports require 'tcp' or 'udp'; 'ip' matches all traffic and can't take a port
options.rationale: Correct: 'eq 23' needs 'tcp'.

options.text: 'eq' must be replaced with 'range'
options.rationale: 'eq' is valid for a single port.

options.text: Port 23 must be written as 'telnet'
options.rationale: Ports can be given by number or by name.

options.text: 120 is a standard ACL number
options.rationale: 100-199 is the extended range.

questions.explanation: Port and protocol keywords: protocols include tcp, udp, icmp, and ip, and operators include eq, neq, gt, lt, and range. Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' matches everything and can't take ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' can't take ports.

questions.stem:
'show access-lists' displays:

Extended IP access list 110
    10 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www (152 matches)
    20 deny ip any any (37 matches)

What can you conclude from this output?

options.text: The ACL's entries and how many packets matched each; it doesn't show where the ACL is applied
options.rationale: Correct: use 'show ip interface' to see the interface and direction.

options.text: ACL 110 is applied inbound on g0/0
options.rationale: This output doesn't show where the ACL is applied.

options.text: Entry 20 is the implicit deny
options.rationale: The implicit deny isn't listed; entry 20 is an explicit deny with its own counter.

options.text: 152 packets were denied
options.rationale: The 152 matches were on the permit entry.

questions.explanation: For verifying ACLs, 'show access-lists' shows what the ACL says and its hit counts; 'show ip interface' shows where it is applied and in which direction.
questions.discriminator_tested: 'show access-lists' = contents and hits; 'show ip interface' = where applied.

questions.stem: An administrator wants ACL 110 to stop filtering on g0/0 for now, but keep the ACL itself for later. Which command does this?

options.text: Under interface g0/0: no ip access-group 110 in
options.rationale: Correct: this removes only the application.

options.text: no access-list 110
options.rationale: This deletes the whole ACL.

options.text: access-list 110 remark DISABLED
options.rationale: A remark only adds a comment; filtering continues.

options.text: Under line vty 0 4: no access-class 110 in
options.rationale: That concerns VTY lines, not the interface filter.

questions.explanation: When removing and documenting ACLs, 'no ip access-group 110 in' removes the application only, 'no access-list 110' deletes the whole ACL, and 'remark' documents entries.
questions.discriminator_tested: Removing the application vs deleting the ACL itself.
